verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal, and the cost falls only on pgbench users who pass -j in init mode. The open points are fixable design points: standards-compat-1 and maintenance-fit-1 concern -j being accepted but silently ignored and the g step depending on the t step. already-exists-1 asks for a comparison with `-I G` that the thread does not have. Only 3 of 20 messages were shown, so confidence is medium.

brief.title: Parallel loading of partitioned pgbench_accounts in pgbench -i
brief.problem: pgbench -i at large scale factors takes a long time, mostly in client-side data generation and vacuum. The author wants faster initialization for people who build benchmark databases. The idea comes from a blog post by Tomas Vondra.
brief.proposed_design: With -j > 1 and --partition-method=range, pgbench -i loads pgbench_accounts with one thread per partition at most. The t step creates parent and partitions as usual. In the g step each worker truncates its assigned partitions and loads them with COPY FREEZE in its own transaction, so vacuum stays cheap.
user_visible_surface: pgbench -j is now accepted in initialization mode and sets the number of loading threads.
Parallel loading applies only with --partitions and --partition-method=range, at most one thread per partition.
author_claims: At scale 100 with 10 partitions, v3 cut total init time from about 29 s to about 13 s.
COPY FREEZE per partition keeps the vacuum phase small (about 1.6 s versus 7.8 s on master).
v5 fixes the --tablespace, -I t then -I G, and repeated -I g failures Koshi reported.
brief.thread_state: Reviewers lakshmi, Hayato Kuroda, Heikki Linnakangas and Koshi Shibagaki took part; v5 is the latest version. Koshi's last message asks to read partition count and bounds from the existing table so -I g alone runs in parallel, and to fall back to serial loading with a message; the author has not replied.
unclear: The patch does not say what happens with -j > 1 and hash partitioning or no partitioning: silent serial load, warning, or error.
No v5 benchmark numbers are posted, and none for hash partitioning or many partitions.
Hayato's worry about memory use with many partitions has no measured answer.
The thread does not say if the separate COPY batching change (Hayato's point 04) is still in the patch.
The thread does not say how -j behaves when the g step runs without the t step in the same invocation, beyond Koshi's report of a silent serial load.

objections.title: No comparison with existing server-side generation (-I G)
objections.failure_scenario: A user who wants a fast large pgbench database can already run `pgbench -i -I dtGvp --partitions=N`, which builds the rows inside the server and sends no COPY data. If G is already close to the parallel g timings, the patch adds thread and connection handling to pgbench but helps few users.
objections.argument: Every timing in messages #1, #9, #12 and #13 compares parallel g against serial client-side g only, and the v5 commit message does the same. Server-side generation (G) is the existing option built to avoid client-side generation cost, and the proposal does not mention it. G does not freeze rows, so parallel g with COPY FREEZE may still win on the vacuum phase, but the thread has no numbers that show this. A committer would likely want this comparison before accepting a second fast-load path in pgbench.
objections.author_must_show: At scale 100 and 2000 with range partitions, how does `-I dtGvp` compare in total time with v5's parallel `-I dtgvp`?

critic.reasoning: No message compares the patch with `-I G`, and server-side generation can produce the same tables. General knowledge suggests G is single-threaded and leaves rows unfrozen, but the thread has no numbers to settle it.

objections.title: -j in init mode is accepted but silently ignored in several cases
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs `pgbench -i -s 1000 -j 16 --partitions=16 --partition-method=hash`, or runs `-I g` against tables made by an earlier `-I dt`. pgbench accepts -j and loads serially without a message. The user finds out only by timing the run or by reading the source.
objections.argument: Before this patch pgbench rejected -j in init mode, so the option failed loudly when it could not apply. The v5 docs promise parallel loading for range partitions, but message #20 shows `-I g` alone loads serially even with --partitions repeated. The docs say nothing for hash or unpartitioned tables, and message #5 already asked why -j is accepted there. The proposal also makes the g step behave differently depending on whether t ran in the same invocation, which breaks the existing independence of -I steps.
objections.author_must_show: For each case where -j cannot parallelize (hash, no partitions, g without t), will pgbench error, warn, or load in parallel, and where is this documented?

critic.reasoning: Message #20 confirms that `-I g` with -j 2 loads serially without a message, and the author has not replied. The v5 docs do not say what -j does with hash partitioning or no partitions.

objections.title: Parallel load depends on t-step state in the same invocation
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs `pgbench -i -I dt --partitions=4`, then later `pgbench -i -I g -s 2 -j 2`. The second run loads serially and gives no message, so the user thinks -j works and only sees it from the timing. A later patch that changes how partition bounds are computed can break the row-to-partition split without any test failing.
objections.argument: Message #20 shows that v5 enables parallel loading only when tables_created is set in the same process, even when --partitions is given again. Koshi notes that the workers' row ranges must match the existing partition bounds, which v5 takes from command-line options and not from the catalog. That couples the g step to the t step. The init steps were meant to be independent, as message #18 points out. The author has not replied to message #20.
objections.author_must_show: Will the g step read partition count and bounds from the existing pgbench_accounts, and will it report when it falls back to serial loading?

critic.reasoning: Message #20 shows v5 derives worker row ranges from command-line options and the tables_created flag, so the g step depends on the t step. The silent serial load overlaps with standards-compat-1, but the open question of reading bounds from the existing table is separate.

refuted.title: -j in init mode can be silently ignored
refuted.failure_scenario: A user with --partition-method=hash, or with no partitions, passes -j 8 to pgbench -i and expects a faster load. Today pgbench rejects -j in init mode. With v5 the option is accepted, the load stays serial, and the user finds out only by comparing timings.
refuted.argument: The v5 docs say -j sets loading threads only with range partitioning, at most one per partition. They do not say what -j does in the other cases. Message #2 shows -j was an error in init mode before, so v5 turns an explicit error into a possible silent no-op. Each later case that gets parallel support, such as hash partitions, adds another branch to this rule, and nothing fails loudly when one is missed.
refuted.author_must_show: What does pgbench -i -j N do with hash partitioning or no partitioning: an error, a warning, or a silent serial load?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same accepted-but-ignored -j cases and adds the confirmed report from message #20.

refuted.title: Speedup reaches only users who already benchmark range-partitioned accounts
refuted.failure_scenario: A user who runs `pgbench -i -s 1000 -j 16` on a plain pgbench_accounts sees no speedup. To get one, they must add --partitions, which changes the schema their benchmark measures. Otherwise they keep the serial load and the existing server-side `-I G` path.
refuted.argument: The general complaint about slow init is real: message #5 says so, and the idea comes from a blog post (message #3). But since v3 (messages #11, #12), the patch helps only --partition-method=range. Every non-partitioned run in the thread is the default layout, and none of those users gain from v5. No message reports someone who builds large range-partitioned pgbench databases often enough for load time to matter, and none compares v5 with `-I G`.
refuted.author_must_show: Who builds large range-partitioned pgbench_accounts today, and how much does v5 save them compared with server-side generation (-I G) at the same scale?

critic.reasoning: The thread weighed the scope: messages #4, #6 and #10 measured the non-partitioned case as no faster overall, and a committer proposed the range-only limit in message #11. Users of plain tables pay no cost, and the `-I G` comparison duplicates already-exists-1.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: pgbench now accepts -j in init mode, with a meaning that depends on partition method and on which init steps run.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: pgbench.c gains a threaded loading path whose row ranges must stay in step with the partition bounds made by the t step.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: pgbench already has server-side generation (`-I G`) as a fast load path, and the thread does not compare against it.

questions: When -j is greater than 1 with hash partitioning, no partitioning, or `-I g` without t, does pgbench raise an error, warn, or load in parallel?
Will the g step read partition count and bounds from the existing pgbench_accounts, so that `-I g` alone can load in parallel?
At scale 100 and 2000 with range partitions, how does total time for `-I dtGvp` compare with v5's parallel `-I dtgvp`?
How much memory does pgbench use during a parallel load with many partitions, for example 1000?
Does v5 still contain the separate COPY batching change that Hayato raised as point 04?

committability.owner_note: Heikki Linnakangas took part in the thread, and the range-only limit came from a committer in message #11. The owner needs to know pgbench's init steps and its thread handling.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a threaded load path in pgbench.c, its behaviour on Windows, and the rule for when -j applies in init mode. The change is client-only, so the liability is limited to pgbench.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted five versions and moved the entry to a new CommitFest in September 2026. Message #20 from Koshi has no reply yet.

priority.reason: The 12.7 KB patch touches only pgbench and helps only users who load range-partitioned pgbench_accounts. The rule for when -j applies and the dependency of the g step on the t step need an answer before more code review.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check how workers map row ranges to partition bounds or what happens to the other workers and their partitions when one worker fails. Only 3 of 20 messages were read in full.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgbench's --partitions option also partition pgbench_history, using the same method as pgbench_accounts. It adds no separate option to turn this on or off.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove redundant initializations
precedents_retrieved.summary: Peter Eisentraut proposed removing code that sets each struct field to zero right after makeNode() or memset() has already zeroed the whole struct. He kept initializations that carry nontrivial comments or keep symmetry between branches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback after waiting on author for three weeks: the patch no longer applied on HEAD, and no rebased version was posted. Before that, Tom Lane objected that explicit initialization of every field is an intended style, which helps when adding a new field and avoids depending on all-zero-bits values. Noah Misch later supported the idea and offered to review it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This has been sitting in the CF app for three weeks waiting on author,
so I have marked this entry as RwF for now:

precedents_retrieved.title: system load consideration hook for parallel workers
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Peter Eisentraut, Tom Lane, Peter Geoghegan
precedents_retrieved.summary: Before starting parallel workers, check the current system load and reduce the number of workers when the system is busy, so parallel query does not slow down other sessions at peak load. The author proposed a hook for this and later posted a POC patch that measures CPU load and picks the worker count from the free CPUs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut argued that a load-based control for parallel workers alone is premature before there is field experience with parallel query, and that the problem covers all process types. He also did not trust system load metrics as a gatekeeper, since load averages lag by about a minute, and found the POC code platform-specific and poorly documented. He suggested refining the existing process-count settings instead, and closed the entry as not favored by the community.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
We don't yet have enough field experience with the parallel query
facilities to know what kind of use patterns there are and what systems
for load management we need.  So I think building a highly specific
system like this seems premature.

precedents_retrieved.title: Lazy JIT IR code generation to increase JIT speed with partitions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch delays JIT IR generation until an expression is first executed, so plan nodes that never run, such as most Parallel Append children over many partitions, are never compiled. A later version also cached the to-be-inlined bitcode modules and cloned them with llvm::CloneModule() instead of reloading them from disk.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected that lazy generation emits roughly one module per function, which is inherently more expensive than emitting one module per query. He would not accept a one-function-per-module design as the base for usage-triggered JIT. He also warned that IRMover renames types in cloned modules, which can degrade code quality. David Geier then found that the module cache had stopped inlining altogether, and that cloning early made llvm::CloneModule() so slow that JIT time stayed high, so he stopped work on it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think that's just inherently more expensive and thus a no-go.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums"
Reverted commit(s): Skip redundant anti-wraparound vacuums
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 2aa6e33, that added a fast path to skip
anti-wraparound and non-aggressive autovacuum jobs (these have no sense
as anti-wraparound implies aggressive).  With a cluster using a high
amount of relations with a portion of them being heavily updated, this
could cause autovacuum to lock down, with autovacuum workers attempting
repeatedly those jobs on the same relations for the same database, that
just kept being skipped.  This lock down can be solved with a manual
VACUUM FREEZE.

Justin King has reported one environment where the issue happened, and
Julien Rouhaud and I have been able to reproduce it in a second
environment.  With a very aggressive autovacuum_freeze_max_age,
triggering those jobs with pgbench is a matter of minutes, and hitting
the lock down is a lot harder (my local tests failed to do that).

Note that anti-wraparound and non-aggressive jobs can only be triggered
on a subset of shared catalogs:
- pg_auth_members
- pg_authid
- pg_database
- pg_replication_origin
- pg_shseclabel
- pg_subscription
- pg_tablespace
While the lock down was possible down to v12, the root cause of those
jobs is a much older issue, which needs more analysis.

Bonus thanks to Andres Freund for the discussion.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P4] (pgbench COPY FREEZE) was withdrawn only because it duplicated another queued patch. [P18] and [P19] are server-side parallel COPY with no recorded reason, and [P1] partitions pgbench_history. None of these reasons applies to client-side parallel loading of pgbench_accounts partitions, and the thread cites no earlier discussion of this idea apart from the blog post in message #3.
The option reuses the existing -j rather than adding a new one, and it was rejected in init mode before, so no existing script changes behaviour. No SQL, catalog or dump surface is involved.

The proposal changes only how the pgbench client loads pgbench_accounts. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or ABI change, and COPY FREEZE after TRUNCATE in one transaction is an existing server path, so this angle has nothing to object to.

The proposal changes no privilege or exposure. Each worker opens a normal client connection with the caller's credentials and runs TRUNCATE and COPY FREEZE on tables that the same user just created. No new privilege, role, or server-side code path is involved, and the connection count is set by the caller through -j and limited to one connection per partition.
Fit and hot path are fine: pgbench is a client tool, and the change adds no server-side cost for users who do not use it. Heikki took part in the thread, so the area has a qualified reviewer.
No extension or external tool that does parallel pgbench initialization is known with certainty. The only existing alternative is pgbench's own server-side generation step, covered above.
Demand for faster pgbench -i in general is plausible and costs fall only on pgbench users, so the only demand concern is the narrow scope of v5.
